body.statement: For every \(S\in\mathcal P_k\), \(\overline W(S)=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}R_{\pi}(S)=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}q_x\min(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in S\})\), and the supremum defining \(\overline W(S)\) is attained by two observationally indistinguishable fixed finite-population response schedules. Consequently \(D^{\star}\) is rational and attained.
body.justification: Two observationally indistinguishable homogeneous arrays in the individual-level \(\Gamma\)-Lipschitz subclass attain the aggregate-class adversarial width, eliminating the response adversary exactly.
body.gap: AnthonyGoyalGuptaNagarajan2010 supplies the robust nearest-facility skeleton and MontielOleaPrallonQiuStoyeSun2025 supplies a causal \(k\)-median analogy; the new result derives these action- and score-specific costs as exact causal diameters.
body.consumer: Trial designers can evaluate every candidate panel without simulating outcomes or solving an inner shape-constrained response program.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(S\in\mathcal P_k\), a compatible table \(y\), a future policy \(\pi\), and a cell \(x\).  Put \(a=\pi(x)\) and \(t=m_\pi\).  If \(T_{xa}(S)=\varnothing\), boundedness of the envelopes gives
\[
u_{xa}(t;y)-\ell_{xa}(t;y)\leq1=r_{\pi x}(S).
\tag{1}
\]
If \(a=a_0\) and \(T_{x a_0}(S)\neq\varnothing\), neutral invariance and compatibility make all neutral anchors equal, so the two neutral envelopes agree and their gap is
\[
0=r_{\pi x}(S).
\tag{2}
\]
Now suppose \(a\neq a_0\) and take any \(c\in T_{xa}(S)\).  If \(m_c\leq t\), the envelope definitions imply
\[
\ell_{xa}(t;y)\geq y_{cx},
\qquad
u_{xa}(t;y)\leq y_{cx}+\Gamma(t-m_c),
\]
while if \(m_c\geq t\), they imply
\[
\ell_{xa}(t;y)\geq y_{cx}-\Gamma(m_c-t),
\qquad
u_{xa}(t;y)\leq y_{cx}.
\]
Together with the unit range of the envelopes, both cases give
\[
u_{xa}(t;y)-\ell_{xa}(t;y)
\leq\min\{1,\Gamma|t-m_c|\}.
\tag{3}
\]
Taking the minimum of (3) over matching anchors, and combining it with (1)--(2), yields
\[
u_{x,\pi(x)}(m_\pi;y)-\ell_{x,\pi(x)}(m_\pi;y)
\leq r_{\pi x}(S).
\tag{4}
\]
Since \(q_x>0\), summing (4), maximizing over the finite nonempty set \(\mathcal F\), and then taking the supremum over \(Y\in\mathcal M_N\) gives
\[
\overline W(S)\leq\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}R_\pi(S).
\tag{5}
\]

For the reverse inequality, finiteness of \(\mathcal F\) supplies a maximizer \(\pi^\star\) of \(R_\pi(S)\).  For each \(x\), write
\[
a=\pi^\star(x),
\qquad t=m_{\pi^\star},
\qquad w=r_{\pi^\star x}(S).
\]
If \(a\neq a_0\) and there is no matching anchor, define \(g_x^-=0\) and \(g_x^+=1\).  If there is a matching anchor and \(w=0\), define both functions to be zero.  In the remaining case \(a\neq a_0\), there is a matching anchor and \(w>0\); then \(\Gamma>0\), and define
\[
g_x^-(s)=\min\{w,\max\{0,\Gamma(s-t)\}\},
\qquad
g_x^+(s)=\min\{w,\max\{0,\Gamma(s-t)+w\}\}.
\tag{6}
\]
Composition with clipping to \([0,w]\) preserves monotonicity and cannot increase a Lipschitz constant, so the functions in (6) are bounded, nondecreasing, and \(\Gamma\)-Lipschitz.  The definition of \(w\) implies
\[
\Gamma|m_c-t|\geq w
\quad\text{for every }c\in T_{xa}(S).
\tag{7}
\]
If \(m_c<t\), equations (6)--(7) give \(g_x^-(m_c)=g_x^+(m_c)=0\); if \(m_c>t\), they give \(g_x^-(m_c)=g_x^+(m_c)=w\).  Equality \(m_c=t\) would imply \(w=0\), excluded in this case.  Hence the two functions agree at all matching anchors and satisfy
\[
g_x^-(t)=0,
\qquad g_x^+(t)=w.
\tag{8}
\]
For \(a=a_0\), use identical zero constants if a matching anchor exists and the two constants zero and one if none exists.  These functions are invariant in score, agree at every selected neutral anchor, and differ at the target by \(w\).

For each cell, use this pair for the target action \(a=\pi^\star(x)\), and use the identical zero function for every other action.  Define homogeneous fixed arrays from these cell surfaces.  The construction is bounded, monotone, \(\Gamma\)-Lipschitz, and neutral-invariant unit by unit; hence both arrays lie in \(\mathcal M_N^{\mathrm{CO},\Gamma}\subseteq\mathcal M_N\).  At every selected arm-cell pair they agree: matching target-action anchors agree by (7)--(8), and all other actions are zero in both arrays.  Denote their common selected table by \(y^\star\).  Their values at \(\pi^\star\) differ by
\[
V_{\mu^+}(\pi^\star)-V_{\mu^-}(\pi^\star)
=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}q_xr_{\pi^\star x}(S)
=R_{\pi^\star}(S).
\tag{9}
\]
The sharp-common-endpoints theorem applied to \(y^\star\) places both values in the same sharp interval, so that interval has width at least (9).  The upper bound (5) forces equality, proves that the supremum is attained, and gives
\[
\overline W(S)
=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}R_\pi(S)
=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}q_x
\min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in S\}\bigr).
\tag{10}
\]
The bridge lemma shows that restricting the supremum in \(\overline W(S)\) to \(\mathcal M_N^{\mathrm{CO},\Gamma}\) leaves it unchanged; independently, the attaining arrays just constructed already lie in that subclass.  Thus (10) is also the exact prospective-width identity over the individual-level Lipschitz refinement.

Every \(q_x=N_x/N\) is rational.  Every \(d_{\pi xc}\) is rational because \(m_c\), \(m_\pi\), and \(\Gamma\) are rational, and all minima, sums, and maxima in (10) range over finite sets.  Hence \(\overline W(S)\) is rational for every panel.  The family \(\mathcal P_k\) is finite and nonempty because it contains \(\varnothing\); therefore its minimum \(D^\star\) is rational and attained.
